learningObjectives.title: What the gold-foil scattering experiment showed and why a nucleus follows
How line spectra show that atomic energy levels are discrete

questions.q: What did Rutherford conclude about the structure of the atom from the results of the Geiger–Marsden experiment?
options: Its nucleus consists of protons and neutrons, which the experiment first detected.
It is a solid ball, and most alpha particles passed through the gaps between the atoms.
Its positive charge and nearly all its mass are in a tiny central nucleus.
Its electrons are heavy enough to turn back any alpha particles that hit them.
optionWhy: A student who credits the whole modern picture of the atom to this experiment picks this. The scattering depends only on the nucleus's charge, mass and size; the neutron was not discovered until 1932.

A student who pictures atoms as solid balls picks this. The foil was many atoms thick, so the alpha particles had to go through the atoms themselves; they passed because each atom is almost entirely empty of mass and concentrated charge.

Only a small, massive, concentrated positive charge can repel an alpha particle strongly enough to turn it back, and the fact that so few were turned back shows that this nucleus fills only a tiny fraction of the atom.
A student who thinks electrons caused the large deflections picks this. An electron has about 1/7300 of the mass of an alpha particle, far too little to reverse its motion.
questions.explain: Only a small, massive, concentrated positive charge can repel an alpha particle strongly enough to turn it back, and the fact that so few were turned back shows that this nucleus fills only a tiny fraction of the atom.

questions.q: White light, containing all visible wavelengths, passes through a cool gas of a single element and is then examined with a spectrometer. What is observed?
options: Dark lines at wavelengths that differ from all of the element's emission lines.
Dark lines at wavelengths that match some of the element's emission lines.
A dark band across every wavelength shorter than the one for the smallest energy gap.
A complete spectrum with no dark lines, as the atoms re-emit all the light they absorb.
optionWhy: A student who thinks absorption is the 'opposite' of emission picks this. The same energy differences are involved, so absorption lines fall at the wavelengths of emission lines.

Atoms absorb only photons whose energy equals a difference between two of their levels. Those are the energies of photons emitted in the reverse transitions, so the dark lines coincide with emission lines; a cool gas absorbs mainly from the ground state, so only some emission lines appear.

A student who thinks an atom absorbs any photon with at least enough energy picks this. A photon is absorbed only if its energy exactly matches a level difference, so separate dark lines appear, not a band.

A student who thinks re-emitted photons continue along the beam picks this. The atoms re-emit in all directions, so the light travelling on towards the spectrometer is depleted at the absorbed wavelengths.
questions.explain: Atoms absorb only photons whose energy equals a difference between two of their levels. Those are the energies of photons emitted in the reverse transitions, so the dark lines coincide with emission lines; a cool gas absorbs mainly from the ground state, so only some emission lines appear.

questions.q: The spectrum of light from a star shows strong dark lines at exactly the wavelengths of the two bright yellow lines in the laboratory emission spectrum of sodium. What can be concluded from this evidence?
options: Sodium is absent from the star, because the light at sodium's wavelengths is missing from its spectrum.
Nothing about sodium, because an element absorbs at different wavelengths from those it emits.
Sodium is the most abundant element in the star, because its absorption lines are so strong.
Sodium atoms in the star's outer layers absorb light at these wavelengths, so sodium is present in the star.
optionWhy: A student who reads a missing colour as a missing element picks this. The light at those wavelengths is missing BECAUSE sodium atoms absorbed it; the dark lines are evidence that sodium is present.
A student who thinks absorption and emission lines of an element differ picks this. The same energy differences give both, so the dark lines coinciding with sodium's emission lines identify sodium.

A student who equates strong lines with large amounts picks this. Line strength also depends on temperature and on how many atoms are in the absorbing level; the lines show that sodium is present, not that it dominates.

Atoms absorb exactly the wavelengths they emit, because the same level differences are involved. Dark lines at sodium's emission wavelengths show that sodium atoms lie in the cooler gas the light passes through, the star's outer layers.
questions.explain: Atoms absorb exactly the wavelengths they emit, because the same level differences are involved. Dark lines at sodium's emission wavelengths show that sodium atoms lie in the cooler gas the light passes through, the star's outer layers.

questions.q: Alpha particles scattered by a thin gold foil are counted at large angles. Up to an alpha-particle kinetic energy E₀ of a few tens of MeV, the counts agree with Rutherford's prediction, which assumes that only the electric repulsion acts. Above E₀ the counts fall below the prediction. Which statement about this result is correct?
options: Below E₀ the alpha particles rebound from the nuclear surface like balls from a wall; above E₀ they break through it, so fewer return.
Above E₀ the electric repulsion no longer acts, and the strong nuclear force alone decides how the alpha particles scatter.
The distance of closest approach of an alpha particle of energy E₀ gives an estimate of the radius of the gold nucleus.
Above E₀ the alpha particles move at nearly the speed of light, so Rutherford's non-relativistic calculation fails.
optionWhy: A student who pictures the nucleus as a hard wall picks this. There is no surface to rebound from: at every energy the deflection is caused by electric repulsion acting at a distance. Within a few femtometres the attractive strong force acts as well, and alpha particles that get this close may be absorbed or take part in nuclear reactions, which is why the counts fall.

A student who thinks one force hands over to the other picks this. The electric repulsion acts at every separation; above E₀ the strong force acts as well, and it is this additional short-range force that makes the electric-only prediction fail.

Deviations begin when the alpha particles get close enough to the nucleus for the short-range strong nuclear force to act. At E₀ the distance of closest approach has become about equal to the nuclear radius, so that distance, found from energy conservation, estimates the size of the nucleus.

A student who reads 'high energy' as 'relativistic' picks this. An alpha particle of a few tens of MeV has kinetic energy about 1% of its rest energy (about 3700 MeV) and moves at roughly 0.1c, so relativistic effects are negligible.
questions.explain: Deviations begin when the alpha particles get close enough to the nucleus for the short-range strong nuclear force to act. At E₀ the distance of closest approach has become about equal to the nuclear radius, so that distance, found from energy conservation, estimates the size of the nucleus.

questions.q: In the Bohr model of hydrogen, what is the angular momentum of the electron in the n = 3 orbit? Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.
optionWhy: The Bohr condition is mvr = nh/2π, so in the n = 3 orbit L = 3h/2π = 3 × 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s/2π = 3.17 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.
A student who carries the n² of the energy formula into the angular momentum calculates 9h/2π = 9.50 × 10⁻³⁴ J s. The angular momentum is proportional to n: mvr = nh/2π = 3h/2π.
A student who gives every orbit the same angular momentum uses h/2π = 1.06 × 10⁻³⁴ J s. That is the value for n = 1 only; in the third orbit mvr = 3h/2π.
A student who writes the condition as mvr = nh, dropping the 2π, calculates 3h = 1.99 × 10⁻³³ J s, 2π times too large. The Bohr condition is mvr = nh/2π.
questions.explain: The Bohr condition is mvr = nh/2π, so in the n = 3 orbit L = 3h/2π = 3 × 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s/2π = 3.17 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.
questions.working: Bohr condition: L = mvr = nh/2π. For n = 3: L = 3 × 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s/2π = 1.989 × 10⁻³³ J s/6.283 = 3.17 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.

questions.q: The masses of a proton, a neutron and a helium-4 nucleus (⁴₂He) are 938.27 MeV c⁻², 939.57 MeV c⁻² and 3727.38 MeV c⁻² respectively. What is the binding energy per nucleon of helium-4?
optionWhy: With masses in MeV c⁻², the mass defect in MeV c⁻² equals the binding energy in MeV: 2(938.27) + 2(939.57) − 3727.38 = 28.30 MeV. Dividing by the 4 nucleons gives 7.075 MeV per nucleon.
A student who treats binding energy and binding energy per nucleon as the same quantity stops at 28.30 MeV. That is the binding energy of the whole nucleus; per nucleon it must be divided by A = 4.

A student who takes the binding energy to be the energy contained in the nucleus divides its rest energy by 4: 3727.38/4 = 931.8 MeV. Binding energy comes from the mass DEFECT, the small difference between the separated nucleons and the nucleus.

A student who reads ⁴₂He as 4 protons and 2 neutrons calculates 4(938.27) + 2(939.57) − 3727.38 = 1904.84 MeV and divides by 6 nucleons. Helium-4 has 2 protons and 2 neutrons; A = 4 is the total number of nucleons.
questions.explain: With masses in MeV c⁻², the mass defect in MeV c⁻² equals the binding energy in MeV: 2(938.27) + 2(939.57) − 3727.38 = 28.30 MeV. Dividing by the 4 nucleons gives 7.075 MeV per nucleon.
questions.working: Mass defect Δm = 2m_p + 2m_n − m_He = 2(938.27) + 2(939.57) − 3727.38 = 3755.68 − 3727.38 = 28.30 MeV c⁻². Binding energy E_b = Δmc² = 28.30 MeV. Helium-4 has A = 4 nucleons, so E_b/A = 28.30 MeV/4 = 7.075 MeV.

questions.q: Approximate binding energies per nucleon are: ²₁H 1.1 MeV; ⁴₂He 7.1 MeV; ²⁸₁₄Si 8.4 MeV; ⁵⁶₂₆Fe 8.8 MeV; ¹¹⁸₅₀Sn 8.5 MeV; ²³⁶₉₂U 7.6 MeV. Which of these processes would release energy?
options: Splitting one ⁵⁶₂₆Fe nucleus into two ²⁸₁₄Si nuclei
Joining two ¹¹⁸₅₀Sn nuclei into one ²³⁶₉₂U nucleus
Separating one ⁴₂He nucleus into its four free nucleons
Fusing two ²₁H nuclei to form one ⁴₂He nucleus
optionWhy: A student who thinks any fission releases energy picks this. Iron-56 is at the peak of the curve; the silicon-28 products have a lower binding energy per nucleon (8.4 MeV against 8.8 MeV), so about 56 × 0.4 ≈ 22 MeV must be supplied.

A student who judges stability by total binding energy notes that one ²³⁶U nucleus (about 236 × 7.6 ≈ 1790 MeV) has more than one ¹¹⁸Sn nucleus (about 1000 MeV). But the two tin nuclei together have about 2010 MeV: forming uranium lowers the binding energy per nucleon from 8.5 MeV to 7.6 MeV and needs about 210 MeV.
A student who thinks binding energy is released when a nucleus is pulled apart picks this. Separating helium-4 into its nucleons needs its whole binding energy, 4 × 7.1 ≈ 28 MeV, to be supplied.
Both deuterium nuclei move far up the binding energy curve: the total binding energy rises from 2 × 2 × 1.1 = 4.4 MeV to 4 × 7.1 = 28.4 MeV, so about 24 MeV is released.
questions.explain: Both deuterium nuclei move far up the binding energy curve: the total binding energy rises from 2 × 2 × 1.1 = 4.4 MeV to 4 × 7.1 = 28.4 MeV, so about 24 MeV is released.
questions.working: Energy is released if the total binding energy (A × binding energy per nucleon) increases. 2 ²H → ⁴He: 4(7.1) − 2 × 2(1.1) = 28.4 − 4.4 = +24 MeV (released). ⁵⁶Fe → 2 ²⁸Si: 56(8.4) − 56(8.8) = −22 MeV (must be supplied). 2 ¹¹⁸Sn → ²³⁶U: 236(7.6) − 236(8.5) = −212 MeV (must be supplied). ⁴He → 4 free nucleons: 0 − 4(7.1) = −28 MeV (must be supplied).

questions.q: A helium-4 nucleus contains two protons and two neutrons. Between which pairs of particles does the strong nuclear force act?
options: Only between a proton and a neutron; two protons or two neutrons do not attract each other.
Between every pair of nucleons: proton–proton, neutron–neutron and proton–neutron.
Between every pair except the two protons, which repel each other as they carry like charges.
Between every pair of nucleons, and between each nucleon and the atom's two electrons.
optionWhy: A student who sees neutrons as the only 'glue' picks this. The strong force acts between any two nucleons, including two protons and two neutrons; the neutrons are not the sole source of attraction.

The strong nuclear force is an attraction between nucleons that does not depend on their charge. It acts between the two protons, between the two neutrons and between each proton–neutron pair, and it is what holds the nucleus together against the electric repulsion of the protons.

A student who thinks the strong force depends on charge, like the electric force, excludes the proton pair. The two protons DO repel electrically, but the strong force between them is attractive and larger at nuclear separations; the strong force takes no account of charge.

A student who thinks the strong force holds the whole atom together includes the electrons. Electrons do not feel the strong force at all: they are held in the atom by the electric attraction of the nucleus, at separations far greater than the force's range.
questions.explain: The strong nuclear force is an attraction between nucleons that does not depend on their charge. It acts between the two protons, between the two neutrons and between each proton–neutron pair, and it is what holds the nucleus together against the electric repulsion of the protons.

questions.q: The four decays below involve nuclides used in medicine and industry. Which decay equation is correct?
options: ¹³¹₅₃I → ¹³¹₅₄Xe + ⁰₋₁e + ⁰₀ν̄
²⁴¹₉₅Am → ²³⁷₉₃Np + ⁴₂α + ⁰₀ν
¹⁸₉F → ¹⁸₈O + ⁰₊₁e + ⁰₀ν̄
⁹⁰₃₈Sr → ⁸⁹₃₉Y + ⁰₋₁e + ⁰₀ν̄
optionWhy: Nucleon number: 131 = 131 + 0 + 0. Charge: 53 = 54 + (−1) + 0. In β⁻ decay a neutron becomes a proton, and an electron and an electron antineutrino are emitted.
A student who adds a neutrino to every decay picks this. The numbers balance, but α decay produces only the daughter and the α particle: ²⁴¹₉₅Am → ²³⁷₉₃Np + ⁴₂α.
A student who pairs the positron with the antineutrino picks this. β⁺ decay emits a positron and an electron NEUTRINO: ¹⁸₉F → ¹⁸₈O + ⁰₊₁e + ⁰₀ν.
A student who thinks a β particle carries away a nucleon lowers A to 89. Nucleon number is then not conserved (90 ≠ 89 + 0). In β⁻ decay A is unchanged: ⁹⁰₃₈Sr → ⁹⁰₃₉Y + ⁰₋₁e + ⁰₀ν̄.
questions.explain: Nucleon number: 131 = 131 + 0 + 0. Charge: 53 = 54 + (−1) + 0. In β⁻ decay a neutron becomes a proton, and an electron and an electron antineutrino are emitted.
questions.working: Iodine-131 (β⁻): 131 = 131 + 0 + 0 and 53 = 54 − 1 + 0, with an antineutrino as required: correct. Americium-241 (α): the numbers balance, but α decay emits no neutrino. Fluorine-18 (β⁺): the numbers balance, but β⁺ decay emits a neutrino, not an antineutrino. Strontium-90 (β⁻): charge balances (38 = 39 − 1) but nucleon number does not (90 ≠ 89 + 0); the daughter is ⁹⁰₃₉Y.

questions.q: A paper mill monitors the thickness of its paper, about 0.1 mm thick, with a radioactive source above the moving paper and a detector below it. The count rate is used to adjust the rollers. Which type of source is most suitable, and why?
options: β⁻, as the paper absorbs part of the β⁻ radiation, and more when it is thicker.
α, as α particles are the most ionizing and also the most penetrating radiation.
γ, as γ rays pass through the paper easily and so give a high count rate.
γ, as γ rays are the least ionizing radiation and so the safest to use.
optionWhy: A thickness gauge needs radiation that the paper absorbs partly. β⁻ particles are partly absorbed by paper, and more are absorbed when it is thicker, so the count rate changes measurably with thickness.

A student who credits α particles with being both the most ionizing and the most penetrating picks this. α particles are the least penetrating: paper stops them all, so the count rate would be background whatever the thickness.

A student who wants the highest count rate picks this. γ rays pass through paper almost unaffected, so a small change in thickness makes almost no change in the count rate; the gauge could not detect it.

A student who ranks hazard by ionizing ability alone picks this. γ rays are also the most penetrating, so they reach workers at a distance, and they are unsuitable anyway because paper hardly absorbs them.
questions.explain: A thickness gauge needs radiation that the paper absorbs partly. β⁻ particles are partly absorbed by paper, and more are absorbed when it is thicker, so the count rate changes measurably with thickness.

questions.q: A detector placed near a source of half-life 2.0 days records 250 counts min⁻¹. With the source removed, it records a background of 50 counts min⁻¹. What will the detector record with the source in the same place 6.0 days later?
options: 75 counts min⁻¹
31 counts min⁻¹
25 counts min⁻¹
50 counts min⁻¹
optionWhy: Only the source's contribution halves. Corrected rate now: 250 − 50 = 200 counts min⁻¹. After 3 half-lives: 200/8 = 25 counts min⁻¹. The detector still records the background too: 25 + 50 = 75 counts min⁻¹.
A student who treats the background as part of the source halves the whole reading three times: 250/8 = 31 counts min⁻¹. Background comes from other sources and stays at about 50 counts min⁻¹.
A student who forgets that the detector always records background gives only the source's contribution, 200/8 = 25 counts min⁻¹. The background of 50 counts min⁻¹ must be added back.

A student who thinks half-life is half the time to decay completely expects the source to be exhausted after 4.0 days, leaving only background. After 6.0 days (three half-lives) the source still gives 25 counts min⁻¹.
questions.explain: Only the source's contribution halves. Corrected rate now: 250 − 50 = 200 counts min⁻¹. After 3 half-lives: 200/8 = 25 counts min⁻¹. The detector still records the background too: 25 + 50 = 75 counts min⁻¹.
questions.working: Corrected count rate now = 250 − 50 = 200 counts min⁻¹. 6.0 days = 3 half-lives, so the corrected count rate becomes 200/2³ = 25 counts min⁻¹. Measured count rate = 25 + 50 = 75 counts min⁻¹.

questions.q: Light stable nuclides have roughly equal numbers of neutrons and protons, but heavy stable nuclides have many more neutrons than protons: ²⁰⁸₈₂Pb has N/Z ≈ 1.5. Why do heavy nuclei need this excess of neutrons to be stable?
options: Extra neutrons add strong-force attraction, which acts only between near neighbours, without adding electric repulsion, which acts between every pair of protons.
The neutrons sit between the protons and shield them from one another's electric repulsion, so more protons need more neutrons between them.
The strong force acts only between a proton and a neutron, so each proton must be surrounded by more than one neutron to be held in place.
The extra neutrons add mass, and the greater gravitational attraction between all the nucleons then holds the larger nucleus together.
optionWhy: The electric repulsion is long-range and acts between every pair of protons, so it grows rapidly as Z increases. The strong force is short-range, so each nucleon is attracted only by its near neighbours. Adding neutrons adds attraction with no extra repulsion, which is what a large nucleus needs to stay bound.

A student who pictures neutrons as insulating spacers picks this. Neutrons do not shield electric forces: the repulsion between two protons is unchanged by what lies between them. Neutrons help by supplying extra strong-force attraction, not by blocking repulsion.

A student who thinks neutrons are the only 'glue' picks this. The strong force acts between all pairs of nucleons, including two protons. Extra neutrons are needed because they add attraction without adding repulsion, not because protons cannot attract each other.

A student who thinks gravity plays a part in binding nuclei picks this. Gravitational attraction between nucleons is about 10³⁶ times weaker than the electric repulsion between two protons and has no role in nuclear stability; the extra binding comes from the strong force.
questions.explain: The electric repulsion is long-range and acts between every pair of protons, so it grows rapidly as Z increases. The strong force is short-range, so each nucleon is attracted only by its near neighbours. Adding neutrons adds attraction with no extra repulsion, which is what a large nucleus needs to stay bound.

questions.q: The binding energy per nucleon peaks at 8.8 MeV for ⁵⁶₂₆Fe and is roughly constant above a nucleon number of about 60, falling slowly to 7.9 MeV for ²⁰⁸₈₂Pb. Which statement is correct?
options: The total binding energy of lead-208 is about 3.3 times that of iron-56, though each nucleon in it is less tightly bound.
The total binding energy of iron-56 is greater than that of lead-208, since its binding energy per nucleon is greater.
The total binding energy of lead-208 is about 14 times that of iron-56, since every nucleon in it attracts every other nucleon.
A lead-208 nucleus stores about 1.6 × 10³ MeV of binding energy, which it releases when it takes part in a nuclear reaction.
optionWhy: Total binding energy = (binding energy per nucleon) × A. For lead-208: 7.9 MeV × 208 = 1.6 × 10³ MeV; for iron-56: 8.8 MeV × 56 = 4.9 × 10² MeV; the ratio is 3.3. Because E_b/A is roughly constant, the total E_b is roughly proportional to A, even though the per-nucleon value is slightly lower for lead.

A student who uses binding energy and binding energy per nucleon interchangeably picks this. Iron-56 has the larger value PER NUCLEON, but lead-208 has almost four times as many nucleons, so its total binding energy (about 1600 MeV) far exceeds iron-56's (about 490 MeV).

A student who assumes the strong force has a long range expects the number of attracting pairs, and so the total binding energy, to grow roughly as A², giving (208/56)² ≈ 14. The near-constant E_b/A shows the total grows in proportion to A, giving a ratio of only about 3.3: evidence that each nucleon is bound only to its near neighbours.

A student who thinks binding energy is energy stored in the nucleus picks this. 1.6 × 10³ MeV is the energy that would have to be SUPPLIED to separate all 208 nucleons; a reaction releases only the difference between the total binding energies of the products and the reactants.
questions.explain: Total binding energy = (binding energy per nucleon) × A. For lead-208: 7.9 MeV × 208 = 1.6 × 10³ MeV; for iron-56: 8.8 MeV × 56 = 4.9 × 10² MeV; the ratio is 3.3. Because E_b/A is roughly constant, the total E_b is roughly proportional to A, even though the per-nucleon value is slightly lower for lead.
questions.working: Total binding energy E_b = (E_b/A) × A. Lead-208: 7.9 MeV × 208 = 1643 MeV ≈ 1.6 × 10³ MeV. Iron-56: 8.8 MeV × 56 = 492.8 MeV ≈ 4.9 × 10² MeV. Ratio = 1643/492.8 = 3.33 ≈ 3.3. (If E_b grew as A², the ratio would be (208/56)² = 13.8 ≈ 14.)

questions.q: The α particles from a given decay to the daughter's ground state all have the same kinetic energy, whereas the β⁻ particles from a given decay have a continuous range of kinetic energies up to a maximum. Which statement correctly explains this difference?
options: α decay produces two bodies, so conservation of momentum fixes the α particle's share of the energy; β⁻ decay produces three, so the electron's share can vary.
Both kinds of particle leave the nucleus with a single energy, but β⁻ particles lose varying amounts of energy in collisions before they escape the source.
Every α decay of a nuclide releases exactly the same energy, but the energy released varies from one β⁻ decay to the next, so the electron's energy varies with it.
The β⁻ particle shares the released energy with a γ photon emitted at the same instant, whereas an α particle takes all of the energy.
optionWhy: With two products, conservation of momentum and energy together fix how the released energy is divided, so every α particle has the same energy. With three products (daughter, electron and antineutrino) the energy can be divided in many ways, so the electron's energy varies from zero up to the maximum, and the antineutrino takes the rest.

A student who looks for an ordinary cause of the spread picks this. The spread is present at emission, and α particles, being far more ionizing, would lose MORE energy in collisions than β⁻ particles, yet their spectrum is discrete. The continuous β⁻ spectrum needs a third particle.

A student who thinks nuclear energy levels are continuous picks this. The daughter nucleus of a β⁻ decay, like that of an α decay, can be left only in discrete energy states, so the energy released is the same in every decay; the variation lies in how it is shared with the antineutrino.

A student who takes the third particle to be a photon picks this. γ photons are emitted later, by an excited daughter nucleus, with discrete energies; they are not produced in every decay. The particle that shares the energy in every β⁻ decay is the antineutrino.
questions.explain: With two products, conservation of momentum and energy together fix how the released energy is divided, so every α particle has the same energy. With three products (daughter, electron and antineutrino) the energy can be divided in many ways, so the electron's energy varies from zero up to the maximum, and the antineutrino takes the rest.

questions.q: Samples X and Y each contain 4.0 × 10¹⁸ undecayed nuclei. The nuclide in X has a half-life of 2.0 h; the nuclide in Y has a half-life of 8.0 h. Which statement about their activities at this instant is correct?
options: Y has four times the activity of X, as its nuclei remain radioactive for longer.
X has four times the activity of Y, as its decay constant is four times larger.
They have equal activities, as they contain equal numbers of nuclei still undecayed.
Their activities cannot be compared, as the decay of each nucleus is random.
optionWhy: A student who links a long half-life with being 'more radioactive' picks this. A longer half-life means a smaller decay constant, so for equal N the activity is SMALLER; Y will simply keep emitting for longer.
A = λN with λ = ln 2/T½. N is the same, and λ for X is ln 2/2.0 h, four times λ for Y (ln 2/8.0 h), so X's activity is four times Y's.
A student who thinks activity depends only on the number of nuclei picks this. A = λN: equal N gives equal activity only for nuclides with the same decay constant.
A student who takes 'random' to mean 'unpredictable in every respect' picks this. With 4.0 × 10¹⁸ nuclei the decay rate is highly predictable: A = λN for each sample.
questions.explain: A = λN with λ = ln 2/T½. N is the same, and λ for X is ln 2/2.0 h, four times λ for Y (ln 2/8.0 h), so X's activity is four times Y's.

questions.q: In the fission ²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n → ¹⁴⁰₅₄Xe + ⁹⁴₃₈Sr + 2¹₀n, the binding energies per nucleon are 7.59 MeV for uranium-235, 8.29 MeV for xenon-140 and 8.59 MeV for strontium-94. A free neutron has no binding energy. Take 1 MeV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ J. How much energy is released in this fission?
optionWhy: A student who subtracts the binding energies per nucleon directly gets 8.29 + 8.59 − 7.59 = 9.29 MeV = 1.49 × 10⁻¹² J. Each value must first be multiplied by its nucleon number to give a total binding energy.

A student who takes the energy released to be the binding energy of the products gives 1968.06 MeV = 3.15 × 10⁻¹⁰ J. The uranium nucleus was already bound by 1783.65 MeV, so only the increase, 184.41 MeV, is released.
The energy released is the increase in total binding energy: [140(8.29) + 94(8.59)] − 235(7.59) = 1968.06 − 1783.65 = 184.41 MeV, which is 184.41 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ J = 2.95 × 10⁻¹¹ J.

A student who thinks the binding energy of uranium is stored in it and released on splitting gives 235 × 7.59 = 1783.65 MeV = 2.85 × 10⁻¹⁰ J. That is the energy needed to separate uranium into free nucleons; fission releases only the gain in binding energy.
questions.explain: The energy released is the increase in total binding energy: [140(8.29) + 94(8.59)] − 235(7.59) = 1968.06 − 1783.65 = 184.41 MeV, which is 184.41 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ J = 2.95 × 10⁻¹¹ J.
questions.working: Total binding energy = A × (binding energy per nucleon). Reactants: ²³⁵U: 235 × 7.59 MeV = 1783.65 MeV; neutron 0. Products: ¹⁴⁰Xe: 140 × 8.29 MeV = 1160.60 MeV; ⁹⁴Sr: 94 × 8.59 MeV = 807.46 MeV; total 1968.06 MeV; neutrons 0. Energy released = 1968.06 MeV − 1783.65 MeV = 184.41 MeV = 184.41 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ J = 2.95 × 10⁻¹¹ J.

questions.q: A sphere of pure uranium-235 has a mass slightly below the critical mass: a chain reaction started in it dies away. Which change, keeping the same mass of uranium-235, could allow it to sustain a chain reaction?
options: Place a strong neutron source beside the sphere so more fissions start
Heat the sphere strongly, so that its nuclei vibrate hard enough to split
Surround the sphere with a material that reflects escaping neutrons back into it
Cut the sphere into small pieces to expose more of its surface to neutrons
optionWhy: A student who thinks the number of starting neutrons decides whether a chain continues picks this. The source starts more chains, but in each one fewer than one neutron per fission causes another fission, so every chain still dies away.

A student who thinks fission is driven by temperature picks this. Nuclei are split by absorbing neutrons, not by thermal motion; heating makes the sphere expand, so its density falls and even more neutrons escape before causing fission.

Below the critical mass too many neutrons escape through the surface. A reflector returns some of them to the uranium, so more neutrons per fission go on to cause fission; enough reflection raises this to one, and the chain becomes self-sustaining.

A student who applies the surface-area rule from chemical reaction rates picks this. Smaller pieces have more surface compared with volume, so even more neutrons escape before causing fission, and the chain dies away faster.
questions.explain: Below the critical mass too many neutrons escape through the surface. A reflector returns some of them to the uranium, so more neutrons per fission go on to cause fission; enough reflection raises this to one, and the chain becomes self-sustaining.

questions.q: Spent fuel contains caesium-137 (half-life 30 years), strontium-90 (half-life 29 years) and technetium-99 (half-life 2.1 × 10⁵ years), produced in similar numbers by fission. Which conclusion about the long-term storage of this waste is correct?
options: After about 60 years, two of their half-lives, the caesium-137 and strontium-90 in it have completely decayed.
Most of its activity at first comes from technetium-99, as it has by far the longest half-life of the three.
Burying it deep in rock reduces its activity, since the rock absorbs the radiation that the waste emits.
It stays radioactive for far longer than 300 years, as the technetium-99 barely decays in that time.
optionWhy: A student who thinks the half-life is half the time to decay completely picks this. After two half-lives a quarter of the caesium-137 and strontium-90 nuclei remain; each half-life halves what is left, so they never decay completely, and the technetium-99 has hardly decayed at all.

A student who thinks a long half-life means high activity picks this. In 30 years half of the caesium-137 nuclei decay but almost none of the technetium-99 nuclei do, so for similar numbers of nuclei far fewer technetium-99 nuclei decay each second, and at first its activity is far smaller.

A student who confuses absorbing radiation with reducing radioactivity picks this. Rock shields people from the radiation, but the number of nuclei decaying per second is unchanged; activity falls only as the nuclei decay.

In 300 years caesium-137 and strontium-90 pass through about 10 half-lives and fall to about 0.1% of their activity, but technetium-99 completes less than 0.2% of one half-life. Its activity persists for hundreds of thousands of years, so containment must last many thousands of years.
questions.explain: In 300 years caesium-137 and strontium-90 pass through about 10 half-lives and fall to about 0.1% of their activity, but technetium-99 completes less than 0.2% of one half-life. Its activity persists for hundreds of thousands of years, so containment must last many thousands of years.
questions.working: After 300 years (about 10 half-lives) the caesium-137 and strontium-90 activities have fallen to about (½)¹⁰ ≈ 1/1000 of their initial values. In 300 years technetium-99 completes only 300/(2.1 × 10⁵) ≈ 0.0014 of a half-life, so almost all of it remains. For similar numbers of nuclei, far fewer technetium-99 nuclei decay each second than caesium-137 nuclei, so its activity is much smaller at first, but it persists for hundreds of thousands of years.

questions.q: At the centre of the Sun the temperature is about 1.5 × 10⁷ K and the density about 1.5 × 10⁵ kg m⁻³. Fusion takes place only in this central core. How, if at all, does the very high density affect fusion in the core?
options: It makes collisions between nuclei frequent enough for fusion to release energy at a high rate.
It brings nuclei close enough together for the gravity between them to pull them into each other.
It has no effect on fusion; only the high temperature of the core affects the rate of fusion.
It gives each nucleus more kinetic energy, which it needs to overcome electric repulsion.
optionWhy: High temperature makes individual collisions energetic enough; high density means many nuclei per cubic metre, so collisions, and hence fusion reactions, happen often enough to release energy at the rate the Sun radiates it.

A student who transfers the role of gravity from the whole star to pairs of nuclei picks this. Between two nuclei, gravity is about 10³⁶ times weaker than their electric repulsion. Gravity acts on the star as a whole, compressing and heating the core.

A student who thinks temperature is the only condition picks this. The rate of fusion also depends on how often nuclei collide; a hot but thin gas has too few collisions to release energy at a significant rate.

A student who runs density and temperature together picks this. The average kinetic energy of the nuclei depends on the temperature; density sets how many nuclei there are per unit volume and so how often they collide.
questions.explain: High temperature makes individual collisions energetic enough; high density means many nuclei per cubic metre, so collisions, and hence fusion reactions, happen often enough to release energy at the rate the Sun radiates it.

questions.q: The diagram shows the spectrum of a star, a continuous spectrum crossed by absorption lines (drawn as gaps in the band), together with the laboratory emission spectra of hydrogen and of sodium drawn to the same wavelength scale. What can be deduced from the diagram?
options: The star's outer layers contain sodium; hydrogen is not detected in them.
Hydrogen atoms in the outer layers are emitting light at those four wavelengths.
The star's core is fusing hydrogen, and that fusion produces the four lines.
The star's outer layers contain hydrogen; no sodium is detected in them.
optionWhy: A student who reads an absorption line as meaning 'this element is absent, so its light is missing' reaches this. An absorption line is produced BY the element: hydrogen atoms in the outer layers absorb light at their own wavelengths, so the absorption lines at hydrogen's wavelengths show that hydrogen is present. The absence of a line at 589 nm means sodium is not detected, not that it is present.

A student who thinks every spectral line is an emission line picks this, but the star's lines are ABSORPTION lines, gaps in the continuous spectrum: less light reaches us at those wavelengths, not more. Hydrogen atoms in the cooler outer layers absorb those wavelengths from the continuous spectrum of the hotter layers beneath. The bright lines are in the laboratory hydrogen spectrum, where a hot gas emits.

A student who takes spectral lines to show what the core is fusing picks this. The lines are formed in the star's outer layers, where atoms absorb light passing outwards; radiation from the core is scattered and re-emitted countless times before it leaves the star and carries no direct record of the fusion reactions. The lines show what the outer layers contain, and nothing about the core.

The star's four absorption lines fall at exactly the wavelengths of the four hydrogen emission lines (410, 434, 486 and 656 nm), so hydrogen in the star's cooler outer layers is absorbing those wavelengths from the continuous spectrum below. There is no absorption line at the sodium wavelength, 589 nm, so the spectrum gives no evidence of sodium in the outer layers.
questions.explain: The star's four absorption lines fall at exactly the wavelengths of the four hydrogen emission lines (410, 434, 486 and 656 nm), so hydrogen in the star's cooler outer layers is absorbing those wavelengths from the continuous spectrum below. There is no absorption line at the sodium wavelength, 589 nm, so the spectrum gives no evidence of sodium in the outer layers.
